title: Napoleon's Sanhedrin (1807)
hookLine: Napoleon questions Jewish leaders about loyalty and law
last: A DOOR OPENED, WITH A PRICE.

cards: A list of questions lands on the table of Jewish leaders gathered in Paris. It comes from the emperor, Napoleon, and it isn't about theology. Does your law allow a man more than one wife?
Is a Jewish divorce valid without the state's courts? May a Jew marry a Christian? Do you consider the French your brothers?
Is France your country, and will you defend it? Underneath them all lies one question: can you be fully Jewish and fully French at the same time? Today, Napoleon's Sanhedrin.

teach.h: AN ASSEMBLY, THEN A GRAND SANHEDRIN.
teach.b: Napoleon first called an assembly of Jewish notables, rabbis and lay leaders, to answer his questions. Then, to give their answers religious weight, he did something theatrical.
He summoned a Grand Sanhedrin, borrowing the name of the ancient high court of Jewish law in Jerusalem, a court of the distant past. How did they answer?
Carefully, and within Jewish law. A man may have only one wife; they pointed to the old ban on taking more. A religious divorce should follow a civil one.

France is our country and we will defend it; the French are our brothers. On marrying Christians they walked a narrow line: such marriages were valid in civil law, while rabbis would not perform them.
Under many answers lay one principle from the Talmud, a saying of the sage Shmuel in Aramaic: dina de-malkhuta dina, the law of the kingdom is the law.
In matters like taxes, property and civil order, Jewish law itself tells Jews to keep the law of the land. That principle was not invented for Napoleon; it was already in the Talmud.
What the Sanhedrin did was draw a line with it. Here, in civil life, the state's law binds us. There, in the commandments between a person and God, our Torah does.
The emperor wanted loyalty. The assembly gave it, and kept back something that was not theirs to give.

teach.h: WHERE LOYALTY LIES, AND WHERE IT STOPS.
teach.b: A loyal question can make you say clearly where your loyalties lie, and where they stop.

how: The Talmudic principle dina de-malkhuta dina is still taught in Jewish law today, as the basis for keeping a country's civil laws, such as paying taxes, alongside the commandments.

games.q: you sit in Napoleon's assembly. the question: is France your country, and will you defend it? what do you answer?
o: no, our only country is the land of Israel.
yes, France is our country and the French our brothers.
games.why: they said France was their country, while keeping the commandments between a person and God for the Torah.

practice: Think of a question about where your loyalties lie, one someone asked you or one you've been avoiding: to a job, a family, a friend, a community, a belief.
Let it sit, then answer the way the Sanhedrin did: carefully, without flattering anyone, saying clearly what you will give and what you will keep; you don't have to say it out loud.

wordCard.voice: Napoleon's Sanhedrin. The Jewish assembly the emperor summoned to answer his questions about loyalty and law, and the Grand Sanhedrin that confirmed its answers. Today's word.

orig.note: Aramaic, from the Talmud: the law of the kingdom is the law.

carryVoice: Your line: loyal questions. The Talmud already had an answer ready. Day nine hundred seventy-four, done.
